clue.text: Double order for lamb, double quick in Chinatown

definitions.meaning: an order of two lamb cutlets at a butcher's counter
pidgin phrase for 'hurry up', associated with Chinese-English speech

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves turn on the same doubled word: two lamb cutlets, and the pidgin call to be quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Two chops make a double order of lamb, and the doubled pidgin word means 'hurry', a phrase from Chinese trade English.

clue.text: Workers love me — because I'm this?

definitions.text: Workers love me — because I'm this?

parts.note: hands are manual workers
love is zero in tennis, the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A good-looking speaker supposes that's why the workers adore them.
explanation.definitionFit: Good-looking people attract admiration, which the speaker thinks explains being loved.

clue.text: This frame-up gets one in anywhere

definitions.meaning: a frame: a mount or tape for framing a picture
a master key that opens every lock

explanation.walkthrough: 'frame-up' looks like a false charge but means something to frame up a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The French term names both a picture mount and a skeleton key, a master key letting its holder pass everywhere.

clue.text: "Chorus —" can't compare with Shelley's skylark

parts.note: in Shelley's 'To a Skylark' a wedding chorus, matched with the bird's song, would be but an empty vaunt; the missing word follows 'Chorus'

explanation.walkthrough: Shelley wrote 'Chorus Hymeneal, / Or triumphal chant, / Matched with thine would be all / But an empty vaunt'; the dash stands for the word after 'Chorus'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means relating to marriage, from Hymen, the Greek god of weddings, as in a wedding chorus.

clue.text: Caustic if paronomastic fellow

parts.note: paronomasia is wordplay, so paronomastic points to a play on words
a gent is a fellow

explanation.surface: A punning man can be biting in his wit.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp, biting remarks are cutting, as an acrid smell is sharp.

clue.text: Young lady, we hear, has success from a bit of foozling

indicators.note: we hear says a word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: miss is a title for a young lady
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: We hear a young woman does well out of some clumsy golf.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'foozle' is to bungle a stroke, especially in golf.
explanation.definitionFit: A bungled stroke that strikes the ball badly is one instance of clumsy play.

clue.text: Eugene's a horned beast

definitions.note: the definition is Eugene's surname, the noun that belongs to him

parts.note: a ram is a horned male sheep

explanation.surface: Eugene is said to own a horned animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Aram was an 18th-century schoolmaster and murderer, subject of Thomas Hood's poem 'The Dream of Eugene Aram'.
explanation.definitionFit: The schoolmaster-murderer Eugene, of Hood's ballad, bore this family name.

clue.text: Bet on Sunshine Boy, a pound — a give-away!

parts.note: taken as written
a ray of sunshine, and Ray is a boy's name
L is the abbreviation for a pound (libra)

explanation.surface: A punter wagers a pound on a horse called Sunshine Boy, and the tip leaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sunshine Boy' is both a sunbeam and the boy's name Ray.
explanation.definitionFit: Treachery gives a secret or a person away, an act of disloyalty.

clue.text: Foreign article one numbers with all created things

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article
the Roman numeral for one is I
numbers in the old sense of metrical lines, poetry

explanation.surface: A foreign piece of writing tallies up everything in creation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' is poetry here (as in 'I lisped in numbers'), not figures.
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmos is the whole of existence, everything that was ever created.

clue.text: Barristers' refreshers here?

parts.note: barristers belong to the four London ... of Court, and a 'refresher' is both a drink and a barrister's extra daily fee; a pub is where one gets refreshment

explanation.walkthrough: A 'refresher' is the further fee paid to counsel for a long case; the barristers' societies in London are the Inns of Court, and pubs sell drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Public houses are places selling refreshment, and lawyers' professional societies in London bear the same name.

clue.text: Husky follower with Thor's weapon delivers pile-driver

parts.note: a sled is what follows a team of husky dogs
the Norse god Thor wields the hammer Mjolnir

explanation.surface: A sled dog's companion wields the thunder god's weapon to deliver a crushing blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy two-handed mallet is used to drive piles and stakes into the ground.

clue.text: Easter-courses for runners ?

definitions.meaning: a church festival whose date changes each year
a meal's courses served to people on the move

explanation.walkthrough: The dash hides a double definition: Easter is the example, and the second half reads the phrase literally as food that travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter falls on a different date each year, the type of a festival with no fixed day; literally a banquet that can be carried.

clue.text: Type of car to hold fifty or two

indicators.note: the car's name is made to hold the numeral inside it

parts.note: a coupé is a two-door car with a fixed roof
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A model of car with room for fifty passengers, or maybe just two.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair is two of something, the same count as a brace.

clue.text: Uncommon vanity it seems from one's horoscope

indicators.note: uncommon suggests something unusual, so the letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Reading your stars seems to bring out an unusual vanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncommon' rearranges VANITY IT. The definition is an old astrological sense: the chart cast for the moment of one's birth.
explanation.definitionFit: In astrology this word names the birth chart, the position of the stars when a person is born.

clue.text: In gay German-English style

annotationWithheld.why: 'In gay German-English style' (7): 'In gay style' gives the answer, but no parse found for 'German-English'; no source gives the setter's intent

clue.text: Bethlehem visitor; can include one conjuror

parts.note: the Magi visited the infant Jesus at Bethlehem

indicators.note: the tin is made to include the numeral within it

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A visitor to Bethlehem; can that include a single conjuror?
explanation.walkthrough: MAGI is plural, though the clue says 'visitor'.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer of tricks and illusions is a conjuror, or a wizard in old tales.

clue.text: Under-cook, soft in the head, turning scales about zero

indicators.note: in the head says the soft sign goes at the front of the word

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft

indicators.note: turning means the zodiac word with its contents is read backwards
about means the star sign goes around the zero

parts.note: Libra is the zodiac sign of the scales
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A cook who is soft in the head and weighs things in circles turns out undercooked food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts O inside LIBRA (LIOBRA); 'turning' reverses that to ARBOIL; P goes 'in the head', in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To boil food partly, leaving it unfinished, is to cook it only part-way.

clue.text: What did Jack break? Give it up!

definitions.text: What did Jack break? Give it up

parts.words: What did Jack break? Give it up
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Jack fell down and broke his crown; to give up a crown is what a monarch does on leaving the throne

explanation.walkthrough: In 'Jack and Jill', Jack 'broke his crown'; giving up the crown is how a king renounces his throne.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch who renounces the throne gives up the crown, formally resigning.

clue.text: Places — for (bovine?) playgoers

explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'in stalls', it is where theatre audiences sit, and where cattle are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up or put in position is to place; and a theatre's front seats and a cowshed's pens share the name 'stalls'.

clue.text: Duck snares 'e set up the grass

indicators.note: set up in a down clue means the run is written upwards, backwards

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nought, O
traps are snares
'e is the dropped-aitch form of 'he', leaving E

explanation.surface: A duck gets caught in traps that he laid in the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses O + TRAPS + E (OTRAPSE).
explanation.definitionFit: This tough grass from Spain and North Africa is used for making paper and rope.

clue.text: Look into severe cuts in American Rubbers.

indicators.note: into puts the word for look inside the cuts

parts.note: deep cuts are gashes
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone inspects deep wounds in an American's rubber tyres.
explanation.walkthrough: In the US 'rubbers' are waterproof overshoes; the surface suggests something else.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call waterproof overshoes 'rubbers', the same footwear as these.

clue.text: Henry gets the bird perhaps, or a mule

definitions.meaning: a cross between Henry and bird: the H and Y of the name with the letters of the bird jumbled
the offspring of a donkey and a horse

explanation.walkthrough: Cross 'Henry' with 'bird' and you get a cross-breed; the letters even mix the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A mule is the cross-bred offspring of a donkey and a mare, the classic example of a crossbreed.

clue.text: Nazi police hide in squirrel's nest-smart!

indicators.note: the police hide in the nest, sitting inside it

parts.note: a drey is a squirrel's nest
the SS were the Nazi paramilitary police

explanation.surface: Nazi police take cover in a squirrel's nest, smartly turned out.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegantly turned out clothing is smart, worn for a formal occasion.

clue.text: Authority left by an anonymous French caller?

definitions.meaning: full power to act as one wishes

definitions.text: left by an anonymous French caller?
definitions.meaning: a visitor leaves a card; in French a blank one would be a 'white card', no name on it

explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase means 'white (blank) card', what a caller who would not give a name might leave.
explanation.definitionFit: A blank cheque of permission gives unlimited authority, and literally it is a blank card in French.

clue.text: Attack cost golfer James his head

indicators.note: cost means losing something, so a letter is taken away
his head points at the first letter of the golfer's name as the one lost

parts.note: James Braid was a Scottish golfer, five times Open champion

explanation.surface: An attack cost a famous golfer his life.
explanation.walkthrough: James Braid (1870-1950) won the Open five times.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden assault on an enemy position is an attack.

clue.text: Skilful-or " canny "?

definitions.meaning: read as 'can-y', having the ability to do something

explanation.walkthrough: 'canny' is read as a made-up adjective from 'can': someone who can.
explanation.definitionFit: A competent person is capable, and one who 'can' is capable too.

clue.text: He profits from his workers' " business "

definitions.text: He profits from his workers' " business "

parts.words: He profits from his workers' " business "
parts.note: the workers are bees and their 'business' is busy-ness, the industry of the hive whose honey the keeper sells

explanation.walkthrough: The workers are worker bees; 'business' in quotes suggests busy-ness, the bees' industry.
explanation.definitionFit: A beekeeper takes the honey made by the worker bees in the hive.

clue.text: How we treat sweated labour is open to question

definitions.note: the definition describes an action, what we do to exploited workers, matching the verb

parts.note: overt means open, not hidden
to ask is to question

explanation.surface: Whether we mistreat exploited workers is open to debate.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description of the verb: what is done to sweated labour is to work it too hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweated labour is exploited, made to work excessively, burdened beyond reason.
